title: Week 9 · Lesson 27: Geriatric Pathophysiology & Clinical Reasoning — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 9 — Lesson 27: Geriatric Pathophysiology & Clinical Reasoning

FNP-level goal: Recognize how frailty, multimorbidity, altered pharmacology, functional decline, and atypical presentation change assessment and disposition in older adults.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate normal aging, frailty, delirium, dementia, depression, and acute medical illness.
  • Assess falls, orthostasis, polypharmacy, cognition, function, and caregiver support.
  • Recognize atypical infection, medication toxicity, and emergency red flags.

Part 1 — Geriatric Syndromes Are Multifactorial

Falls, frailty, delirium, incontinence, functional decline, and polypharmacy often result from multiple small vulnerabilities rather than one isolated diagnosis. A minor infection, missed meals, dehydration, a new sedating medication, pain, or environmental hazard can precipitate major loss of function.

In older adults, “what changed from baseline?” is often the most important question.

Part 2 — Frailty and Reduced Reserve

Frailty is decreased physiologic reserve and increased vulnerability to stressors. It may present as weakness, slowed gait, exhaustion, low activity, weight loss, recurrent falls, or delayed recovery. Frailty does not mean inevitable decline; it means that illness, hospitalization, and medication changes can cause disproportionate harm.

FNP assessment includes ADLs/IADLs, mobility, nutrition, cognition, mood, sensory impairment, social support, advance-care goals, and caregiver strain.

Part 3 — Delirium Versus Dementia

Delirium is acute, fluctuating inattention and altered awareness caused by an underlying physiologic disturbance. Infection, medication toxicity, withdrawal, hypoxia, dehydration, urinary retention, constipation, pain, metabolic disease, and neurologic events are common contributors. It is an emergency until the cause is identified.

Dementia is a chronic progressive cognitive syndrome; it does not explain an abrupt change. A patient with dementia can also develop superimposed delirium.

Part 4 — Falls Are a Symptom, Not a Diagnosis

A fall may result from syncope, orthostasis, arrhythmia, stroke/TIA, seizure, medication effect, neuropathy, vision impairment, gait/balance disorder, environmental hazard, acute illness, or interpersonal harm. Ask about circumstances, prodrome, loss of consciousness, head strike, anticoagulants, injuries, prior falls, footwear, assistive device, alcohol/substances, and ability to get up.

Assess gait, balance, strength, orthostatic blood pressure, vision, feet/footwear, home hazards, and medications. A fall with head injury, new neurologic deficit, syncope, persistent pain, inability to bear weight, or anticoagulant use may require urgent evaluation.

Part 5 — Polypharmacy and Pharmacologic Vulnerability

Age-related renal/hepatic changes, altered body composition, and multiple prescribers increase risk of accumulation, interactions, delirium, hypotension, bleeding, falls, and hypoglycemia. Medication reconciliation must include prescription drugs, OTC products, alcohol, supplements, dosing adherence, and recent changes.

Ask for each drug: What is the indication? Is it effective? Is it causing harm? Is the dose appropriate for kidney/liver function? Can it be simplified or deprescribed safely with the prescriber?

Part 6 — Orthostasis, Syncope, and Cardiovascular Risk

Orthostatic symptoms can reflect dehydration, autonomic dysfunction, blood loss, infection, medication effect, or cardiac disease. Measure orthostatic vital signs when appropriate and review antihypertensives, diuretics, sedatives, anticholinergic burden, and glucose-lowering therapy. Do not label a syncopal event “a mechanical fall” without considering cardiac and neurologic causes.

Part 7 — Infection and Atypical Presentation

Older adults may present with delirium, functional decline, anorexia, falls, weakness, or tachypnea instead of high fever. A positive urine test alone does not prove symptomatic UTI; correlate with compatible symptoms and a full differential. Conversely, do not dismiss new confusion or weakness as aging when infection, sepsis, stroke, or medication toxicity is possible.

Part 8 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 1

An 84-year-old with baseline mild dementia becomes abruptly inattentive, sleepy, and unable to transfer after a new opioid and poor oral intake. Reasoning: acute delirium with medication/dehydration and medical causes. Decision: urgent assessment, medication review, vital signs, and source evaluation.

Part 9 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 2

A 76-year-old has two falls, dizziness when standing, new diuretic dose, reduced urine output, and orthostatic symptoms. Reasoning: possible volume depletion/medication-related hypotension, but assess arrhythmia, bleeding, infection, and neurologic causes.

FNP High-Yield Framework

Acute change = delirium/medical cause until proven otherwise.
Falls = multifactorial assessment, not a diagnosis.
Medication review = diagnostic and preventive intervention.
Function and supports determine whether an outpatient plan is safe.
